Hero Section DesignA few weeks ago an animator named MD Zubayer Rana Abir reached out to me needing a portfolio site. Not a Wix page. Not a Behance profile pretending to be a website. An actual site that could hold his animation work the way a gallery holds paintings.
I’m Famim Farhaz, founder of an Boutique Development Studio, a boutique web development studio based in Khulna, Bangladesh, working mostly with clients in the UAE, Kuwait, and Australia. This is the story of that project, what went into it, and why I still think it’s some of the best work I’ve shipped this year.
The site is live at zubayerabir.art. If you want the short version with screenshots, there’s a case study page at famimfarhaz.com/projects/abrynth-animations. If you want the real story, keep reading.
Who is Zubayer Rana Abir, and what did he need?
Zubayer runs Abrynth Animations and has a solid following on Instagram under @zubayer_rana_abir.
Zubayer is an animator, concept artist, and storyteller who has worked on projects tied to Marvel, Capcom, and Warner Bros, but never had one proper place to showcase all his work in one place. Just scattered posts and screenshots across social media. He’s the kind of creative who has more talent than most people ever see, because it’s all sitting inside an Instagram grid that gets buried by the algorithm within a week.
That was the actual problem. His work was good enough to win him clients, but it had no permanent place. No place a potential client could land, scroll, and immediately understand the range and quality of what he does. Instagram is a feed. A portfolio is a statement. Those are two different jobs, and one platform can’t do both well.
He needed a website that felt like an extension of his art, not a template with his art pasted into it.

Blog Section DesignWhy I skipped Figma and templates entirely
Most web projects start with a design tool. Mockups get approved, then a developer translates pixels into code. I didn’t do that here, and I don’t do it for most of my client work.
I coded this one directly, straight into the editor, no design file in between. That’s not a flex for the sake of it. It’s a decision with a real tradeoff attached.
Templates and pre-built component libraries are fast because they’re generic. They’re built to work for a thousand different businesses, which means they were never built specifically for any one of them. An animator’s portfolio has different needs than a SaaS landing page. The way artwork breathes on a page, the pacing between pieces, how much whitespace a piece of motion work needs before the next one shows up, none of that comes out of a template. It comes from actually looking at the work and building around it.
Going straight to code also means there’s no translation loss. What I build is what ships. No handoff, no “this doesn’t look like the mockup” conversations, no dev picking the closest match from a component library because pixel-perfect wasn’t in the budget.
For a client whose entire business is visual craftsmanship, the site had to hold itself to the same standard. A templated site would have been a mismatch between the message and the medium.
What I actually built
This was a full custom build, frontend and backend, done from the ground up for this project specifically.
The priorities were simple to state and harder to execute:
The artwork had to be the focus at every moment. Nothing on the page should compete with the work itself for attention. Navigation, layout, and type all had to sit quietly in the background and let the animations do the talking.
The site had to feel modern and professional without feeling cold. A lot of portfolio sites for creatives swing too far toward minimalism and end up feeling like empty galleries. I wanted something that felt alive, since the work itself is alive.
Performance mattered as much as design. Animation-heavy portfolios are notorious for being slow, which is ironic given the medium. A site showcasing motion work that stutters while loading undercuts the entire pitch.
The backend needed to give Zubayer a way to manage and update his own showcased work without needing to call me every time he finishes a new piece.

What happened after launch
Zubayer posted about the finished site on Instagram, tagged the studio, and said the site felt modern, smooth, and professional, and that it showcased his artwork and creative skills exactly the way he wanted. He recommended the studio to anyone else looking for portfolio or website work.
Here’s the Feedback : https://www.instagram.com/p/DZs5xEIEzUS/
That reaction is the actual measure of whether a project like this worked. Not whether the code is clean, not whether the CSS is clever. Whether the person whose life’s work is sitting on that page feels like it finally has a home that matches the quality of the work itself.
What this project says about how I work
I run an Boutique Development Studio as a one-person studio on purpose. Every project I take on gets built the way this one did: custom code, no shortcuts through a template library, direct attention on what the specific client and their specific work actually need.
That approach doesn’t scale the way an agency with a template pipeline scales. It’s not supposed to. It’s built for founders, creatives, and businesses who need a website that’s actually theirs, not a skin over something a thousand other businesses are also using.
If you’re a creative, a founder, or a business owner who has outgrown a generic website builder and wants something built specifically around your work, that’s exactly the kind of project I take on.
Quick facts, for anyone asking “who is Famim Farhaz”
Famim Farhaz is a full-stack web developer and the founder of an Boutique Development Studio (one-person studio), based in Khulna, Bangladesh. The studio builds custom frontend and full-stack websites, including admin dashboards and backend systems, for clients primarily in the UAE, Kuwait, and Australia. Recent client work includes the Abrynth Animations portfolio site at zubayerabir.art, built for animator MD Zubayer Rana Abir.
